1000052.etyen:
Internationalism, French Gabon, from Portuguese Gabão, originally the Portuguese name of the estuary now known as the Gabon Estuary. Portuguese navigators arriving on the coast in the fifteenth century called the estuary Rio de Gabão (“Gabon River”), from gabão (“hooded cloak, overcoat”), because its distinctive shape was thought to resemble such a garment.
The French name was subsequently extended from the estuary to the surrounding colonial territory, and the modern country consequently takes its name from the Gabon Estuary.
Ultimate origin of Portuguese gabão uncertain. Dicionário Infopédia

1000308.etyen:
Borrowed from French -ine (“chemical-substance-forming suffix”), from Latin -īna (“feminine form of -īnus”), the feminine of -īnus (“of or pertaining to”), from Proto-Italic *-īnos, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *-iHnos. Some learned formations also reflect Ancient Greek -ινος (-inos, “of or pertaining to”).
Compare Danish -in and Swedish -in, as well as English -ine, French -ine and German -in (“chemical-substance-forming suffix”).

1004404.etyen:
From an old genitival form of the river name now represented by Kinso, and vík (“bay, cove”), hence “the bay of Kinso”. The river name is related to kinn (“cheek; steep mountainside”), referring to the steep-sided valley through which the river flows.
The name originally belonged to the farm and parish where Kinsarvik Church was built, and was subsequently transferred to the settlement and municipality. The historical spelling Kinservik was replaced by Kinsarvik as the official municipal spelling in 1917.
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk Kinsarvik (“village, parish and former municipality”).
